memories.title: National Ascension Monument
memories.summary: Atatürk monument in the middle of Cumhuriyet Meydanı, Antalya's main civic square. The sculptor was Hüseyin Gezer and it was unveiled in 1964.
details: Atatürk stands at the top of a rising rock-like base, with a boy and a girl beside him for the nation's youth.
The levels of the base stand for the steps from 19 May 1919 to the founding of the Republic.
Photographed on Republic Day, 29 October, with the square hung with flags.

media.alt: Sculpture group on a rocky base in Cumhuriyet Meydanı under a grey sky, with a tall Turkish flag and flag bunting across the square

memories.title: Hadrian’s Gate
memories.summary: Marble triumphal arch with three openings, built in 130 CE for Emperor Hadrian's visit to the city, then called Attaleia. It is now the main entrance to the old town, Kaleiçi.
details: A large restoration finished in 1959. Dark granite and white marble columns now stand side by side, and sources disagree on which are original.
The two towers beside the arch were not part of the first plan.
Ancient fragments are displayed on the lawn in front, including a spiral-fluted column. Where they were found was not confirmed.

media.alt: Weathered stone tower beside the arches of Hadrian’s Gate, with ancient column pieces on the lawn in front
Spiral-fluted stone column standing on the grass, with carved blocks and the tower and arch behind it

memories.title: Perge
memories.summary: Ruins of a major city of ancient Pamphylia. The entrance is the Hellenistic Gate, two round towers from the 3rd century BCE, with a marble colonnaded street running on beyond it.
details: The horseshoe-shaped courtyard behind the gate was redesigned in the early 2nd century CE. Inscriptions link it to the benefactress Plancia Magna.
The colonnaded street runs about 300 m with a water channel down the middle and ends at a nymphaeum, a monumental fountain from Hadrian's time.
The city declined in the Byzantine period as the Aksu river silted up.

memories.title: Kaleiçi old town
memories.summary: Antalya's old town inside the city walls, with red-tiled roofs stepping down toward the sea. Its best-known landmark is the fluted brick Yivli Minaret, from the 13th century.
details: The Yivli Minaret is about 38 m tall, brick above a cut-stone base, with eight flutes that give it its name.
It belongs to a complex that also holds the Yivli Mosque, a madrasa and a Mevlevi lodge.
The second view looks over the roofs toward the sea.

media.alt: Fluted brick minaret rising above red-tiled roofs and trees, with a stone mosque, a clock tower and domes beyond, under grey cloud
Red-tiled roofs and whitewashed houses stepping down toward the sea under heavy cloud

memories.title: Hıdırlık Tower
memories.summary: Round stone tower on a square base where Kaleiçi meets Karaalioğlu Park, floodlit at night. Its foundations may date to the 1st or 2nd century CE.
details: About 14 m high, standing in a small park.
Its first purpose is uncertain. The usual view is a tomb for an important person, and it may later have served as a lookout or lighthouse over the harbour.

media.alt: Floodlit round stone tower on a square base at night, with glass railings in front and café lights to the right

memories.title: Sultanyar Kebap
memories.summary: Kebap house in Antalya whose signature dish is the Sultanyar Special mixed grill. The menu says it has been open since 1979.
details: Starters came to the table before ordering: çiğ köfte, a herby yogurt dip, acılı ezme, butter, greens and fresh sesame flatbread.
The two-person Special was skipped to leave room for lahmacun.
The menu marks allergens and calories beside each dish.

memories.title: Around Antalya
memories.summary: Everyday scenes from walking around the city: the bay, a painted bike path and a café stop. Not tied to one named site.
details: The bay view looks across the water to mountains, with a boat leaving a white wake.
The bike path is painted blue and yellow beside a road with taxis.
At a café in the evening a kitten curled up on a lap.

memories.title: Köfteci Cihat
memories.summary: Lunch after Perge at a köfte restaurant in Aksu: soup, grilled köfte on flatbread, a hummus-style plate, a rocket and tomato salad and ayran.
details: The köfte came on flatbread with a grilled green pepper and onions.
The restaurant is Köfteci Cihat, found from the name and the Aksu branch near Perge. The Maps link could not be opened to confirm the branch.

memories.title: Aspendos Theatre
memories.summary: One of the best-preserved Roman theatres anywhere, built in the reign of Marcus Aurelius by the local architect Zenon. The stage building still stands, which is rare.
details: Built between 161 and 180 CE. Two brothers, Curtius Crispinus and Curtius Auspicatus, are named as the commissioners.
Sources disagree on capacity: figures range from about 7,000 to 13,000 and 12,000 for the 41 rows of seats.
In the 13th century the Seljuks turned the stage building into a palace, and the theatre was also used as a caravanserai.
A modern stage platform and protective covers were in place, because the theatre is used for opera and ballet performances.
Cats wander the site. The last two photos show a black-and-white cat with her kittens on the old paving.

memories.title: Aspendos upper city ruins
memories.summary: Ruined walls and arches above the theatre in low evening light, with grass, broken columns and a carved cornice still in place.
details: The photos show a tall ruined wall with decorated stonework, a large arched hall open to the sky and a row of broken column bases.
Which building each ruin was is not confirmed here.

memories.title: Karadeniz Balıkçısı
memories.summary: Fish restaurant in Side where dinner was a big plate of fried anchovies with a table of small side dishes. The photo menu is shown with it.
details: The big plate looks like hamsi tava, fried anchovies, listed at 500 TL on the menu.
The table also had a green salad, bread, lemon, pickles, radish, cucumber, cherry tomatoes and two dips.
The menu lists the address as Side Cad. No:40, Manavgat, Antalya.

memories.title: Breakfast before Side
memories.summary: Breakfast before walking round the ancient town of Side. The spinach pancake was the favourite.
details: Menemen came in a copper pan, with a spinach gözleme, an omelette, olives, tomato and Turkish coffee.
The spinach pancake was really good.

memories.title: Side ancient city
memories.summary: The Roman theatre and restored columns of Side under restoration, a clifftop by the sea with an old motorbike, and a pomegranate eaten inside the old walls.
details: Theatre: built in the second half of the 2nd century CE, possibly on an earlier Hellenistic theatre.
Estimates put the theatre seating at about 13,700 to 17,200 people. The upper rows sit on two levels of barrel-vaulted arches.
In late Roman times a wall was built around the orchestra to make an arena for gladiator fights and animal shows.
The hoardings show aerial photos of the theatre and the name Side Antik Kenti.
Columns: fluted marble columns stand again on new bases, with a steel scaffold holding a stack of stone beams behind.
A sign on the hoarding behind lists the Temple of Demeter, but which building these columns belong to is not confirmed here.
The first column photo is a weathered column drum on its base, with the grain of the fluting still visible.
Seafront: an old motorbike parked on a dusty clifftop beside the sea, with a tour boat on the horizon and a rain cloud over the water.
A bare tree, an old drum and a few ancient stone slabs frame the spot.
Pomegranate: Side is known as an old pomegranate town, so they ate one there, cut open at a table under the trees beside the old walls.
Side’s name is said to come from an ancient local word for pomegranate, and the city took the fruit as its symbol.

memories.title: Olympos
memories.summary: A Lycian city in a forested valley, split by a creek that runs down to the sea. The photos cover the Roman temple’s monumental door, the harbour tomb, the Episcopal Palace, tombs and inscriptions, and a clip from the entrance.
details: Overview: a Hellenistic city and member of the Lycian League, with its earliest city wall dating to around 300 BC. The pirate leader Zenicetes held it as a stronghold. It came under Roman rule in 77 BC, and Hadrian visited in 129 AD. It was at its height in the 5th and 6th centuries AD, then in decline after Arab raids in the 7th century.

Roman temple (the monumental entrance): the site board says it was built in the first half of the 2nd century AD under Hadrian, in the centre of the northern city, and was the most important building in the city, probably built to honour the emperor’s visit. The walls of the sacred chamber (naos), the pronaos up to floor level and part of two columns survive.

Temple façade: built entirely of cut stone blocks, with six Ionic columns in front, friezes of curling branches and rosettes, a flat-faced pediment, and lion-head gargoyles on the sides. The columned front has collapsed. Blocks found in excavations since 2017 are displayed around the temple.
The naos façade wall and the monumental door, with its cantilevered lintel, survive with elaborate carving. On some blocks the decoration was left unfinished.

Episcopal Palace: in the Byzantine period the temple area became a bishop’s palace, and the temple building, still standing, became part of it. Four piers were added to the naos and a door was opened to connect it with the space to the west.

The palace sits in the centre of the northern city at a junction of main streets, was enclosed by a perimeter wall, and is the largest structure in the city, a rectangle of about 128 by 62 m. It took in the earlier Roman temple and its temenos (or forum).

Inscription at the Episcopal Palace: a Greek text on a wall block names a Marcus Aurelius Zosas (also called Aristandros) and a Menodoros (also called Lysimachos), both Olympians, and mentions the pankration, the ancient combat sport. It may honour an athlete or a gift in someone’s memory. This is a tentative reading from a photo, not a translation.

Tomb inscription: a sarcophagus carries a Greek notice naming a man from Olympos who built the tomb for himself, his children and his brothers, and barring anyone else from being buried in it. A fine is payable to the treasury, with a third part in the final line. The photo is partly broken, so this is a rough reading, not a translation.
Entrance complex: ruined rubble-stone walls with a lintel doorway, standing among pines below the forested slopes.

Bath house: Wei was told these ruins are a bath house said to have been built by the emperor Vespasian. This is not confirmed here: a general history of Olympos only says that public buildings such as baths lay in the southern part of the city.

Still on the list: the basilica and the building with mosaics, the sarcophagus of Antimachos, the theatre across the river, and the acropolis for the view. The Chimaera flames (Yanartaş) are a short hike away and are best near dusk.

Harbour tomb: a captain’s sarcophagus with a ship carved on its front, a face in the pediment of its lid, and a mosaic floor in front. One guide says it is the sarcophagus of Captain Eudemos, with an inscription about his voyages. The name comes from that one guide and is not confirmed here.
